name: Passive, conditionals and reported speech
intro: Three grammar structures that make your English more flexible: the passive voice, conditional sentences with “if”, and reported speech.
sammendrag:
## The passive voice

In an **active** sentence, the subject does the action: **The chef cooked the meal.** In a **passive** sentence, the focus moves to what the action is done to: **The meal was cooked (by the chef).**

The passive is formed with **be + past participle**: is made, was built, has been sold, will be announced. We use it when the doer is unknown, unimportant or obvious: **My bike was stolen.** English is made in many countries. It is also common in news and science: **The results were published yesterday.** Do not overuse it – active sentences are usually clearer.

## Conditional sentences

Conditional sentences describe what happens if something else happens. They have an **if-clause** and a **main clause**.

- **Zero conditional** (always true): If you **heat** ice, it **melts**. (present + present)
- **First conditional** (real possibility in the future): If it **rains** tomorrow, we **will stay** inside. (present + will)
- **Second conditional** (unreal or unlikely now): If I **had** a million kroner, I **would travel** the world. (past + would)
- **Third conditional** (unreal past): If she **had studied**, she **would have passed**. (had + past participle + would have)

A common mistake is putting “would” in the if-clause: “If I would have money” is wrong – it should be “If I had money”. In formal English, “If I **were** you, I would…” is used with all persons.

## Reported speech

**Direct speech** repeats someone's exact words: She said, “I am tired.” **Reported speech** (indirect speech) retells what someone said: She said (that) she **was** tired.

When the reporting verb is in the past (said, told, asked), the verb in the reported sentence usually moves **one step back** in time:

- am/is → was, do → did, will → would, can → could
- have done → had done, did → had done

Pronouns and time words also change: “I will call you **tomorrow**” → He said he would call me **the next day**. Questions become statements: “Where do you live?” → She asked where I **lived**. For yes/no questions, use **if** or **whether**: He asked **if** I liked football.

## Why learn this?

These structures let you vary your writing, express possibilities and wishes, and retell conversations and sources accurately – skills you need in essays, articles and discussions.

flashcards.def: The subject does the action: The chef cooked the meal.
Focus on what the action is done to: The meal was cooked.
be + past participle: is made, was built, has been sold.
When the doer is unknown, unimportant or obvious; common in news and science.
Always true: If you heat ice, it melts.
Real future possibility: If it rains, we will stay inside.
Unreal now: If I had money, I would travel.
Unreal past: If she had studied, she would have passed.
Say “If I had money”, not “If I would have money”.
Formal form used with all persons in the second conditional.
Someone's exact words in quotation marks: “I am tired.”
Retelling what someone said: She said she was tired.
In reported speech, the verb moves one step back: will → would, is → was.
Time words change in reported speech.
Use if or whether: He asked if I liked football.

options: The man was bitten by the dog.
quiz.explain: The passive uses be + past participle (was bitten), and the focus is on the man.

quiz.text: Make the sentence passive: “Someone stole my bike.”
quiz.explain: was + past participle (stolen). We leave out “by someone” because it adds nothing.

quiz.text: Which conditional is this? “If it rains tomorrow, we will stay inside.”
quiz.explain: It describes a real possibility in the future: present + will.

quiz.text: Complete: “If I … a million kroner, I would buy a house.”
quiz.explain: The second conditional uses the past tense in the if-clause: If I had…

quiz.text: Complete: “If she … harder, she would have passed the test.”
quiz.explain: The third conditional uses had + past participle in the if-clause.

quiz.text: Change to reported speech: She said, “I am tired.”
quiz.explain: The pronoun changes (I → she) and the verb moves back (am → was).

quiz.text: Change to reported speech: He said, “I will call you.”
options: He said he will call me.
He said he would call me.
He said he called you tomorrow.
quiz.explain: “Will” becomes “would”, and the pronouns change to fit the new speaker.

quiz.text: How do you report the question “Do you like football?”
options: He asked do I like football.
He asked did I like football?
He asked that I like football.
He asked if I liked football.
quiz.explain: Reported yes/no questions use if/whether and normal statement word order.

quiz.text: Which zero conditional sentence is correct?
options: If you heat ice, it melts.
If you heated ice, it would melt yesterday.
If you will heat ice, it melts.
If you heat ice, it would melt.
quiz.explain: The zero conditional uses present + present for things that are always true.

quiz.text: When is the passive especially useful?
options: When you want to be informal
When the doer is unknown or unimportant
quiz.explain: “The window was broken” works well when we do not know or care who broke it.

ekstra.text: “If I would have time, I would help you” is correct.
ekstra.explain: We do not use “would” in the if-clause. Correct: If I had time, I would help you.

ekstra.text: The passive is formed with a form of “be” and the past participle.
ekstra.explain: Examples: is made, was built, has been sold.

ekstra.text: Passive sentences are always clearer than active sentences.
ekstra.explain: Active sentences are usually clearer. Use the passive when there is a reason to.

ekstra.text: Which sentence is the second conditional?
options: If I win, I will celebrate.
If I won, I would celebrate.
If I had won, I would have celebrated.
ekstra.explain: The second conditional: past in the if-clause + would.

ekstra.text: Make passive: “They build new houses every year.”
options: New houses were building every year.
New houses are built every year.
New houses have build every year.

ekstra.text: Report: “Where do you live?” she asked.
options: She asked where do I live.
She asked where did I live.
She asked if where I lived.
ekstra.explain: The question word stays, the word order becomes a statement, and the verb moves back.
